extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy critics, performance students, and readers interested in humor theory and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing stand-up that intentionally subverts traditional joke form to address trauma and marginalized experience, following the approach Hannah Gadsby uses in Nanette. Focus is on whether the piece completes 'half-told' stories, critiques its own form, and produces ethical/audienced-level change rather than mere laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of joke form to deliver something more than a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comedian use joke form to deliver something more than a joke?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gadsby's approach repurposes setup/punchline mechanics: the setup creates tension and the expected punchline releases it, but the comedian uses that form to deliver material that isn't merely a laugh — e.g., testimony, critique, or sustained grief. Evaluate whether the piece intentionally leverages joke structure to carry non-comedic content (tragedy, critique) rather than only seeking release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing the 'half-told story'
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a half-told story being completed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often truncates traumatic experience into a brief setup and punchline, creating a 'half-told story.' The work should return to those same stories and tell the rest — giving trauma the space and complexity jokes normally deny. Check for explicit revisiting or extension of earlier anecdotes so that the audience receives the fuller, complicated account rather than an 'easy punchline.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of its own form (breaking the joke contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work critique its own form?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nanette breaks the implicit 'joke contract' (setup>punchline>release) mid-performance. Assess whether the piece self-reflexively exposes how jokes are constructed, how they function socially, and whether it deliberately abandons expected punchlines to make a critical point about comedy itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling marginalized experience with full complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is marginalized experience handled with full complexity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the performance resists reducing marginalized lived experience to a single gag. Avoiding flattening, stereotyping, or simplifying trauma is central: the work should resist turning systemic harm into merely a device for laughter and should present nuance, context, and the ongoing harms involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding self-deprecating humor that compounds harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the piece refrain from self-deprecating moves that add to existing insults?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-deprecating humor can be 'doubly painful' for marginalized people because it invites the audience to join the chorus of insults. Check whether the comedian uses self-belittlement to placate audiences or whether they refuse that valve, instead refusing to join the bullies or to make their own oppression the tidy target of a laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural innovation (intentional two-part or disruptive form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the structure intentionally shift (e.g., first half conventional, second half disruptive) to reframe earlier material?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gadsby's pattern: first half uses traditional jokes (e.g., coming-out anecdotes), second half returns to those stories to reveal trauma and stop being 'funny.' Assess whether the piece employs a deliberate structural pivot that reframes earlier jokes as wounds rather than punchlines and whether that pivot is clear and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of whose tension is being released
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the performance recognize who benefits from the laughter and whose tension is being used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes create and release tension; evaluate whether the comedian is aware that marginalized performers often learned to release the audience's tension (representing others' pain). The criterion asks whether the work foregrounds that dynamic and refuses to be merely the instrument of others' relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility about whose pain becomes a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work take responsibility for whether it turns others' pain into laughter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gadsby's Nanette forces the industry to reckon with which harms are being appropriated for laughs. Assess whether the piece interrogates the morality of converting real suffering into comedic material and whether it offers alternatives or reparative framing rather than exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience transformative impact (not just relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience emerge changed, not just relieved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond momentary catharsis, the work should aim to alter audience perspective, empathy, or behavior. Evaluate whether the performance leaves audiences unsettled, reflective, or moved in ways that extend past laughter — i.e., the goal is transformation rather than merely tension release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical moves (e.g., announcing 'quitting') as argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the performance use declarations (such as 'quitting') rhetorically rather than literally to signal a new mode?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gadsby's announced quitting functions as a rhetorical device to mark a break from prior modes of joke-making. Check whether similar dramatic claims in a performance are used to signal formal or ethical shifts instead of being straightforward actions, and whether they productively frame the work's aims.
